segment:
Jonah let go with a smile and gestured to the couch. “Here’s my spot, it’s all yours.”
It turned out he was a fellow visitor, an engineer from Georgia who would be leaving tomorrow night. That was all she could find out while they were alone.
The other two men, Jonah said, were Adrian and a man named Robert who had come up from Southern California. And a young woman would be coming too, “I’m afraid,” said Jonah, “but she’s wonderful.” They would be here by six thirty.
Mara was not afraid of the young woman. The thought that there would be more people here, any people, was already relaxing her. She sat down on the far end of the couch.
Jonah stood there for a while longer, leaning against the wall with his ankles crossed and watching her. He looked like he might take another seat, but he stayed where he was. They spoke about this and that: how long Jonah would be staying, how far each had come, what they knew about Fulcrum—but nothing much came of it. They were both just feeling their way.
Then Mara noticed that someone else had walked in and was standing in the doorway, watching them too.
A tall man, older, with short curly gray hair and a tweed jacket, stood there observing Mara and Jonah. He glanced down at Mara’s hand, still clutching the strap of her duffel bag, and raised an eyebrow. He said nothing.
He was probably the Robert that Jonah had mentioned.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

segment:
Jonah smiled and let go, taking a step back and turning toward the couch as he did so. “Come sit,” he said over his shoulder. She did.
She sat.

It was all a bit awkward. He had introduced himself like a guest and then treated her like one. She couldn’t figure out if that meant she wasn’t one, if it was just manners, or if they were both guests and they were supposed to be making this easy for each other.
Jonah had sat back down on the couch with his bare feet propped up again, not so relaxed as he’d been when she came in but not especially tense either. He wasn’t fidgeting at all; he was just sitting there, looking at her from across the low table. She wasn’t sure what to do next.

“You’re a bit young,” he commented in a conversational way, as if it were a fun thing for them to be able to talk about.
“You are too,” she said after a pause, not knowing quite how to feel about the remark.
He blinked at that and laughed. “Yeah, I suppose I am.”

There was a silence in which Jonah appeared to be considering something else to say.
After a minute, she cleared her throat. “Am I too young?”

He cocked his head to one side. “It depends who you ask,” he said, half-smiling. “What do _you_ think?”
She shrugged. “I don’t know,” she said in a conversational way. “You tell me.”
